hints: Count the longest carbon chain that contains the C=C bond and number it so the double bond gets the lowest possible locant.
walkthrough:
Read the skeleton**
Look at T. The double bond is in the middle with two methyl groups on each C of the C=C. The longest chain through the double bond has 4 carbons, so the parent is but-2-ene.

Add the branches**
There is one methyl substituent on C2 and one on C3. Combine this with the parent to give $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C=C(CH}_3\text{)}_2$ named as 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene.

hints: T cannot show cis-trans isomerism because each C of its C=C has two identical methyl groups, so think what feature a C=C needs to show cis-trans isomerism.
walkthrough:
Recall the condition for geometrical isomerism**
For cis-trans isomerism each carbon of the C=C must carry two different groups. In T each $\text{C}$ has two $\text{CH}_3$ groups, so it cannot do this. You need a different $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}$ alkene where this condition is met.

Pick a valid isomer**
A simple choice is hex-3-ene: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Each C of the double bond has H and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, two different groups, so cis and trans forms exist. In skeletal form this is a zig-zag of 6 vertices with a double line in the centre.
Final answer: Skeletal formula of any one of: cis-hex-3-ene or trans-hex-3-ene or 4-methylpent-2-ene or 3-methylpent-2-ene, drawn with zig-zag skeletal lines and C=C shown.

hints: Remember sigma bonds lie directly between nuclei, while the pi bond in C=C comes from sideways overlap above and below the C-C axis.
walkthrough:
Picture the sigma framework**
The diagram already shows the sigma bonds in the plane using wedges and dashes. The two C atoms of the double bond are already joined by a sigma bond along the C-C axis.

Add the pi electron cloud**
Each C also has an unhybridised p orbital at right angles to that axis. Draw one lobe above and one lobe below on each C, overlapping sideways. This sideways overlap is the $\pi$ bond, sitting above and below the $\text{C-C}$ line.
Final answer: Two p-orbitals, one on each C of C=C, overlapping sideways above and below the sigma bond axis to form the pi bond.

hints: Count the sigma bonds plus lone pairs around each doubly bonded C to find the number of electron pairs that determines hybridisation.
walkthrough:
Count regions around C=C carbons**
Each doubly bonded C in T joins to three other atoms by sigma bonds and has no lone pairs. Three sigma regions means three hybrid orbitals are needed.

Link to hybridisation**
Three hybrid orbitals comes from mixing one s and two p orbitals, which is $\text{sp}^2$ hybridisation. The remaining p orbital forms the $\pi$ bond.

hints: Reaction 1 converts C=C in T to two C-OH groups on adjacent carbons to give diol U, so recall which mild oxidising agent does syn dihydroxylation.
walkthrough:
Recognise the transformation**
T, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=C(CH}_3)_2$, becomes U, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C(OH)-C(OH)(CH}_3)_2$. This is addition of two OH groups across the double bond to make a diol.

Recall the reagent**
Mild oxidation with cold dilute acidified potassium manganate(VII) gives the diol. Hot concentrated conditions would cleave the molecule further, so cold and dilute is essential.
Final answer: Cold, dilute, acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$

hints: Recall what colour precipitate 2,4-DNPH gives with any aldehyde or ketone.
Think what functional group must be present in V for that positive result to appear.
walkthrough:
State the observation**
2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine reacts with carbonyl compounds to form a brightly coloured solid hydrazone. With V you see a yellow, orange or red precipitate.

Explain the inference**
Only aldehydes and ketones give this result. V is $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-CO-CH}_3$, a ketone, so the precipitate proves the $\text{C=O}$ carbonyl group is present in the product.

Final answer: Add 2,4-DNPH gives a yellow / orange / red precipitate.
This confirms V contains a carbonyl group, C=O.

hints: Compare functional groups in U (a diol) and V (a ketone) and list which bonds are lost and which are formed.
Recall the characteristic IR wavenumber ranges for an alcohol C-O stretch and a ketone C=O stretch from the Data Booklet.
walkthrough:
Track bonds that change**
U has two $\text{C-O}$ single bonds from its OH groups, V has one $\text{C=O}$ double bond and no $\text{C-O}$. Ignore $\text{O-H}$ because water solvent masks it.

Assign IR bands**
The $\text{C-O}$ stretch at 1040-1300 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ will shrink or vanish as U is consumed. The $\text{C=O}$ stretch at 1670-1740 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ will grow as V forms. Watching those two bands monitors the reaction.

Final answer: C-O absorption in range 1040-1300 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ decreases / disappears as alcohol groups are lost.
C=O absorption in range 1670-1740 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ appears / increases as ketone forms.

hints: Reaction 3 uses alkaline aqueous iodine with V, a methyl ketone, so recall the classic observation for this iodoform reaction.
walkthrough:
Spot the methyl ketone**
V is $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-CO-CH}_3$. It has a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO-}$ group, which gives a positive iodoform reaction with alkaline $\text{I}_2$.

State the observation**
Both V and W are colourless and soluble, but the iodoform product $\text{CHI}_3$ is an insoluble pale yellow solid, so you observe a yellow precipitate.
Final answer: Yellow precipitate

hints: In reaction 3 the organic molecule is oxidised to a carboxylate, so decide which other reactant must gain electrons.
walkthrough:
Apply redox logic**
Reaction 3 is redox. The methyl ketone V is oxidised to carboxylate W plus iodoform. Oxidation must be paired with reduction.

Identify the oxidant**
Alkaline aqueous $\text{I}_2$ acts as the oxidising agent, so $\text{I}_2$ itself is reduced to $\text{I}^-$ (found in $\text{CHI}_3$ and $\text{NaI}$). Hydroxide is base, not redox.
Final answer: Iodine, $\text{I}_2$

hints: Reaction 4 reduces the ketone C=O in V to CH-OH in X, so count how many [H] atoms are needed to add across C=O.
walkthrough:
See the change**
V, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$, is a ketone. $\text{NaBH}_4$ supplies hydride, written as $[\text{H}]$, to reduce $\text{C=O}$ to $\text{CH-OH}$ to give alcohol X, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$.

Balance with [H]**
Forming $\text{CH-OH}$ from $\text{C=O}$ needs two H atoms, one on C and one on O. So: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O} + 2[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$$

hints: Draw the structure of X, 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol, and locate the carbon bonded to four different groups.
Recall how a pair of enantiomers is drawn with solid wedge and dashed wedge bonds swapped around the chiral centre.
walkthrough:
Find the chiral centre**
X is $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-CH(OH)-CH}_3$. Look at C2: it holds $\text{C(CH}_3)_3$, $\text{OH}$, $\text{CH}_3$ and H, four different groups, so it is chiral and exists as two enantiomers.

Draw mirror images**
Draw C2 with solid wedge for one group, e.g. $\text{CH}_3$, and dashed wedge for H, with $\text{OH}$ and $\text{C(CH}_3)_3$ in the plane. For the second isomer swap the wedge and dash, putting H on a solid wedge and $\text{CH}_3$ on a dashed wedge. The two are mirror images.

Final answer: Two 3D structures of $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C-CH(OH)-CH}_3$ that are non-superimposable mirror images: chiral C with $\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_3$, $\text{OH}$, $\text{CH}_3$ and H, with wedge and dash positions reversed between the two drawings.

hints: Reaction 5 is dehydration of a secondary alcohol to an alkene, so recall the strong acid dehydrating agent and the need for heat.
walkthrough:
Recognise dehydration**
X, an alcohol, loses $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to give alkene Y. This is acid catalysed elimination.

Give reagents**
Use concentrated sulfuric acid or concentrated phosphoric acid with heat. Dilute acid or cold conditions would favour substitution, not elimination.
Final answer: Heat with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ or concentrated $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$

hints: Write out monomer Y, 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene, and remember the double bond opens to form two single bonds in the polymer chain.
walkthrough:
Open the double bond**
Y is $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH-C(CH}_3)_3$. In addition polymerisation the $\pi$ bond breaks and each monomer links by new sigma bonds to neighbours.

Draw the repeat**
The repeat unit becomes $-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(C(CH}_3)_3)-$. Show short continuation bonds at each end through the backbone carbons to indicate the chain continues.
Final answer: Repeat unit: $-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH(C(CH}_3\text{)}_3)-$ with continuation bonds through the chain.

hints: Think why many addition polymerisations need heat, pressure or a catalyst even though they are exothermic overall.
walkthrough:
Link rate to energy barrier**
At room temperature molecules have low average kinetic energy. Breaking the $\pi$ bond to start the chain and forming the reactive intermediate needs a large initial energy input.

Conclude**
Because the activation energy for initiation of addition polymerisation is high, few collisions succeed at room temperature, so reaction 6 is very slow without heating, pressure or an initiator/catalyst.
Final answer: High activation energy
